To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the evolution of GALM in larval helminths is a consequence of the interaction between the mortality and growth functions of the larva, and the life cycle strategy of the parasite.
the optimal strategy for a larval parasite in a host with time-dependent mortality is to grow until the death rate is constant, and then stop growing.
the evolutionarily stable strategy for a larva in an intermediate host is to grow until GALM, but in a paratenic host is to stop growing as soon as it can.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the complex life cycles of helminths, which are often trophically transmitted, with the larva passing through one or more intermediate hosts before entering the definitive host.
the conditions favouring the evolution of growth arrest, and the evolution of growth to a size at which death rate becomes constant.
the evolution of life history strategies in trophically transmitting helminth larvae.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimal growth strategy for a given species depends on its life cycle, and that the life cycle is a consequence of the optimal strategy.
the conditions for GALM are more likely when the larva is in an intermediate host than when it is in a paratenic host.
paratenic and intermediate hosts are both optimal strategies, and which is adopted is determined by the relative importance of the various parameters in the two types of host.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the conditions favouring parthenic hosts are those that favour rapid transmission to a host where the larva can grow to maturity.
GALM and no growth are favoured by high mortality and low growth in the intermediate host, and low mortality and high growth in the definitive host.

, in the absence of GALM, growth in intermediate hosts is favoured if the larval mortality in the definitive host is high, and if there are few larvae in the definitive host when the larvae in the intermediate host are established.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GALM is a common strategy for trophically transmitted parasites, and it has evolved independently in several taxa, including nematodes, trematodes and acanthocephalans.
the decision of whether to grow or not is a complex one that depends on the details of the mortality functions and on the parameters in each of the hosts.
the evolution of GALM in trophically-transmitted helminths is not a simple consequence of host resource limitation, but depends on many factors.
